claim: Chlamydia trachomatis (Ctr) can persist over extended times within their host cell and thereby establish chronic infections.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis (Ctr) can persist over extended times within their host cell and thereby establish chronic infections.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about Chlamydia biology.

claim: IFN-γ is one of the major inducers of chlamydial persistence.
source: One of the major inducers of chlamydial persistence is interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) released by immune cells as a mechanism of immune defence.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and established knowledge in the field.

claim: IFN-γ activates the catabolic depletion of L-tryptophan (Trp) via indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), resulting in persistent Ctr.
source: IFN-γ activates the catabolic depletion of L-tryptophan (Trp) via indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), resulting in persistent Ctr.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism in the field, supported by citations in the manuscript (Taylor and Feng, 1991).

claim: IFN-γ induces the downregulation of c-Myc in a STAT1-dependent manner.
source: Here, we show that IFN-γ induces the downregulation of c-Myc, the key regulator of host cell metabolism, in a STAT1-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1I demonstrating STAT1 signaling and c-Myc downregulation.

claim: Expression of c-Myc rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence in cell lines.
source: Expression of c-Myc rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence in cell lines and human fallopian tube organoids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-C showing rescue of bacterial growth and infectious progeny formation.

claim: Expression of c-Myc rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence in human fallopian tube organoids.
source: Expression of c-Myc rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence in cell lines and human fallopian tube organoids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D-E showing rescue in organoid models.

claim: Trp concentrations control c-Myc levels most likely via the PI3K-GSK3β axis.
source: Trp concentrations control c-Myc levels most likely via the PI3K-GSK3β axis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E showing phosphorylation of GSK3β and c-Myc levels in response to Trp addition.

claim: Ctr infection reprograms the host cell tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle to support pyrimidine biosynthesis.
source: Unbiased metabolic analysis revealed that Ctr infection reprograms the host cell tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle to support pyrimidine biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A-B demonstrating changes in TCA cycle intermediates.

claim: Addition of TCA cycle intermediates rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence.
source: Addition of TCA cycle intermediates or pyrimidine/purine nucleosides to infected cells rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6D-H showing rescue with α-ketoglutarate and citrate.

claim: Addition of pyrimidine/purine nucleosides to infected cells rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence.
source: Addition of TCA cycle intermediates or pyrimidine/purine nucleosides to infected cells rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6D-F showing rescue with nucleosides.

claim: Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases (STD), with more than 130 million new cases annually.
source: It is the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted diseases (STD), with more than 130 million new cases annually (Newman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Newman et al., 2015.

claim: Infection of the urogenital tract by Chlamydia can lead to urethritis, infertility, ectopic pregnancies, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).
source: Infection of the urogenital tract by Chlamydia can lead to urethritis, infertility, ectopic pregnancies, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) (Malik et al., 2009; Svenstrup et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Malik et al., 2009 and Svenstrup et al., 2008.

claim: Left untreated, Chlamydia infection increases the risk of HIV infections.
source: Furthermore, left untreated, Chlamydia infection increases the risk of HIV infections (Galvin and Cohen, 2004; Ho et al., 1995) and might contribute to the development of cervical and ovarian cancer (Gagnaire et al., 2017; Hare et al., 1982; Koskela et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Galvin and Cohen, 2004 and Ho et al., 1995.

claim: Chlamydia infection might contribute to the development of cervical and ovarian cancer.
source: Furthermore, left untreated, Chlamydia infection increases the risk of HIV infections (Galvin and Cohen, 2004; Ho et al., 1995) and might contribute to the development of cervical and ovarian cancer (Gagnaire et al., 2017; Hare et al., 1982; Koskela et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gagnaire et al., 2017; Hare et al., 1982; Koskela et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2004 and uses speculative language ('might').

claim: The pathogen extensively interferes with the physiology of the infected cell, since it depends entirely on its host cell as a replicative niche during infection.
source: The pathogen extensively interferes with the physiology of the infected cell, since it depends entirely on its host cell as a replicative niche during infection (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Chlamydiae have a unique biphasic life cycle, consisting of two physiologically and morphologically distinct forms.
source: Chlamydiae have a unique biphasic life cycle, consisting of two physiologically and morphologically distinct forms (Gaylord, 1954).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gaylord, 1954 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Elementary bodies (EB) are the non-dividing infectious form of Chlamydia.
source: This gram-negative bacterium initiates its developmental cycle by attachment and invasion of the host cell by the elementary body (EB), the non-dividing infectious form of the pathogen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydia biology.

claim: EB differentiate into reticulate bodies (RB), which is the non-infectious replicating form of the pathogen.
source: EB differentiate into reticulate bodies (RB), which is the non-infectious replicating form of the pathogen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydia biology.

claim: EB stay within the endosomes, which they modify rapidly to create a replicative niche termed 'inclusion', to avoid lysosomal degradation.
source: Inside the cell, EB stay within the endosomes, which they modify rapidly to create a replicative niche termed 'inclusion', to avoid lysosomal degradation (Hackstadt et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hackstadt et al., 1997.

claim: Chlamydia progenies are released by host cell lysis or extrusion, an exocytosis like mechanism, to infect neighbouring cells.
source: It takes several rounds of cell division until RB re-differentiate back into EB and the progenies are released by host cell lysis or extrusion, an exocytosis like mechanism, to infect neighbouring cells (Abdelrahman and Belland, 2005; Hybiske and Stephens, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Abdelrahman and Belland, 2005 and Hybiske and Stephens, 2007.

claim: During the persistent state, the pathogen remains viable and replicates its genome, but it exhibits decreased metabolic activity and inhibited cell division, which leads to the formation of enlarged pleomorphic aberrant bodies (AB).
source: During the persistent state, the pathogen remains viable and replicates its genome, but it exhibits decreased metabolic activity and inhibited cell division, which leads to the formation of enlarged pleomorphic aberrant bodies (AB) (Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wyrick, 2010.

claim: The transition to the persistent form might represent an important chlamydial survival mechanism against antibiotics and the immune response of the host, since this process is reversible.
source: The transition to the persistent form might represent an important chlamydial survival mechanism against antibiotics and the immune response of the host, since this process is reversible (Beatty et al., 1994; Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beatty et al., 1994 and Wyrick, 2010, and uses speculative language ('might').

claim: The conversion to the dormant stage is induced by penicillin.
source: The conversion to this dormant stage is induced by penicillin (Tamura and Manire, 1968), iron deficiency (Raulston, 1997), amino acid starvation (Allan and Pearce, 1983b), and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) (Beatty et al., 1994; Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tamura and Manire, 1968.

claim: The conversion to the dormant stage is induced by iron deficiency.
source: The conversion to this dormant stage is induced by penicillin (Tamura and Manire, 1968), iron deficiency (Raulston, 1997), amino acid starvation (Allan and Pearce, 1983b), and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) (Beatty et al., 1994; Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Raulston, 1997.

claim: The conversion to the dormant stage is induced by amino acid starvation.
source: The conversion to this dormant stage is induced by penicillin (Tamura and Manire, 1968), iron deficiency (Raulston, 1997), amino acid starvation (Allan and Pearce, 1983b), and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) (Beatty et al., 1994; Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Allan and Pearce, 1983b.

claim: The conversion to the dormant stage is induced by interferon-gamma (IFN-γ).
source: The conversion to this dormant stage is induced by penicillin (Tamura and Manire, 1968), iron deficiency (Raulston, 1997), amino acid starvation (Allan and Pearce, 1983b), and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) (Beatty et al., 1994; Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beatty et al., 1994 and Wyrick, 2010.

claim: IFN-γ is an immune-regulated cytokine, which is involved in the cell-intrinsic immunity against several intracellular pathogens, including Chlamydia.
source: IFN-γ is an immune-regulated cytokine, which is involved in the cell-intrinsic immunity against several intracellular pathogens, including Chlamydia (MacMicking, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to MacMicking, 2012.

claim: The downstream signalling pathways activated by IFN-γ are highly species specific and differ dramatically between mouse and human cells.
source: The downstream signalling pathways activated by IFN-γ are highly species specific and differ dramatically between mouse and human cells (Nelson et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nelson et al., 2005.

claim: In human cells, the anti-chlamydial effect of IFN-γ is predominantly mediated by the induction of indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO).
source: In human cells, the anti-chlamydial effect of IFN-γ is predominantly mediated by the induction of indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), an enzyme that catalyses the initial step of L-tryptophan (Trp) degradation to N-formyl kynurenine and kynurenine (Taylor and Feng, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Taylor and Feng, 1991.

claim: IDO catalyses the initial step of L-tryptophan (Trp) degradation to N-formyl kynurenine and kynurenine.
source: In human cells, the anti-chlamydial effect of IFN-γ is predominantly mediated by the induction of indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), an enzyme that catalyses the initial step of L-tryptophan (Trp) degradation to N-formyl kynurenine and kynurenine (Taylor and Feng, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Taylor and Feng, 1991 and represents established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Ctr as a Trp auxotroph needs to take up Trp from the host cell for its development.
source: Ctr as a Trp auxotroph needs to take up Trp from the host cell for its development (Østergaard et al., 2016; Wyrick, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Østergaard et al., 2016 and Wyrick, 2010.

claim: Trp depletion by IFN-γ treatment leads to persistence.
source: Trp depletion by IFN-γ treatment therefore leads to persistence (Beatty et al., 1994; Byrne et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beatty et al., 1994 and Byrne et al., 1986.

claim: Ctr contain a tryptophan synthase operon comprised of genes encoding the tryptophan repressor (TrpR) and tryptophan synthase α and β subunits (TrpA and TrpB, respectively).
source: However, Ctr contain a tryptophan synthase operon comprised of genes encoding the tryptophan repressor (TrpR) and tryptophan synthase α and β subunits (TrpA and TrpB, respectively) (Fehlner-Gardiner et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fehlner-Gardiner et al., 2002.

claim: Chlamydia with an intact tryptophan synthase operon have been shown to produce Trp from indole, a metabolic activity that can rescue these strains from IFN-γ-induced growth restriction, if indole is available at the site of infection.
source: Chlamydia with an intact tryptophan synthase operon have been shown to produce Trp from indole, a metabolic activity that can rescue these strains from IFN-γ-induced growth restriction, if indole is available at the site of infection (Caldwell et al., 2003; Ziklo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Caldwell et al., 2003 and Ziklo et al., 2016.

claim: IFN-γ belongs to the type II interferons that bind to the extracellular domain of the IFN-γ receptor, which is a heterodimer of the two subunits IFNGR1 and IFNGR2.
source: IFN-γ belongs to the type II interferons that bind to the extracellular domain of the IFN-γ receptor, which is a heterodimer of the two subunits IFNGR1 and IFNGR2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN-γ signaling.

claim: The intracellular domains of the IFNGR1 subunits are associated with Janus kinase 1 (Jak1), while the IFNGR2 subunits are associated with Jak2.
source: The intracellular domains of the IFNGR1 subunits are associated with Janus kinase 1 (Jak1), while the IFNGR2 subunits are associated with Jak2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN-γ signaling.

claim: Activation of Jak1 and Jak2 results in phosphorylation of the receptor and subsequent recruitment and phosphorylation of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT1).
source: Activation of Jak1 and Jak2 results in phosphorylation of the receptor and subsequent recruitment and phosphorylation of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN-γ signaling.

claim: STAT1 phosphorylation at tyrosine 701 and serine 727 leads to its homodimerization and nuclear translocation.
source: STAT1 phosphorylation at tyrosine 701 and serine 727 leads to its homodimerization and nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about STAT1 signaling, supported by citations in the manuscript (Hu and Ivashkiv, 2009; Krause et al., 2006; Ramana et al., 2000).

claim: Once in the nucleus, STAT1 homodimers bind to IFN-γ-activated sequence (GAS) elements in the promoters of target genes to regulate their transcription.
source: Once in the nucleus, STAT1 homodimers bind to IFN-γ-activated sequence (GAS) elements in the promoters of target genes to regulate their transcription (Hu and Ivashkiv, 2009; Krause et al., 2006; Ramana et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hu and Ivashkiv, 2009; Krause et al., 2006; Ramana et al., 2000.

claim: IFN-γ can function as both a growth inhibiting and promoting cytokine in a STAT1-dependent manner.
source: IFN-γ can function as both a growth inhibiting and promoting cytokine in a STAT1-dependent manner (Asao and Fu, 2000; Ramana et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Asao and Fu, 2000 and Ramana et al., 2000.

claim: Binding of STAT1 homodimers to the consensus GAS elements in the c-myc promoter inhibits its expression transcriptionally.
source: Binding of STAT1 homodimers to the consensus GAS elements in the c-myc promoter inhibits its expression transcriptionally (Ramana et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ramana et al., 2000.

claim: c-myc expression is not only negatively regulated by STAT1 but stat1 is also a negative target gene of c-Myc.
source: Concurrently, c-myc expression is not only negatively regulated by STAT1 but stat1 is also a negative target gene of c-Myc.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schlee et al., 2007.

claim: c-Myc and STAT1 regulate each other in a negative feedback loop at the transcriptional level.
source: Hence, c-Myc and STAT1 regulate each other in a negative feedback loop at the transcriptional level (Schlee et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schlee et al., 2007.

claim: The transcription factor c-Myc targets genes involved in the regulation of numerous cellular processes, such as cell proliferation, cell growth, translation, metabolism, and apoptosis.
source: The transcription factor c-Myc targets genes involved in the regulation of numerous cellular processes, such as cell proliferation, cell growth, translation, metabolism, and apoptosis (Battey et al., 1983; Coffin et al., 1981; Dang, 1999; Duesberg and Vogt, 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Battey et al., 1983; Coffin et al., 1981; Dang, 1999; Duesberg and Vogt, 1979.

claim: c-Myc activity increases energy production, anabolic metabolism, promotion of aerobic glycolysis, and glutaminolysis, inducing mitochondrial biogenesis and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity.
source: Furthermore, c-Myc activity increases energy production, anabolic metabolism, promotion of aerobic glycolysis, and glutaminolysis, inducing mitochondrial biogenesis and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity (Dang, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dang, 1999.

claim: Glutaminolysis increases the production of biomass by providing TCA cycle intermediates via anaplerosis, which enhances their availability for the production of amino acids, nucleotides, and lipids.
source: Glutaminolysis increases the production of biomass by providing TCA cycle intermediates via anaplerosis, which enhances their availability for the production of amino acids, nucleotides, and lipids (Kress et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kress et al., 2015.

claim: c-Myc critically controls nucleotide biosynthesis by directly regulating the expression of genes that encode the enzymes involved in the production of precursors of all nucleotides.
source: c-Myc also critically controls nucleotide biosynthesis by directly regulating the expression of genes that encode the enzymes involved in the production of precursors of all nucleotides (Liu et al., 2008; Mannava et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2008 and Mannava et al., 2008.

claim: c-Myc directly controls the cis-regulatory element in the 5'-UTR of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase, which catalyses the first committed step in purine biosynthesis.
source: For example, c-Myc directly controls the cis-regulatory element in the 5'-UTR of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase, which catalyses the first committed step in purine biosynthesis (Cunningham et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cunningham et al., 2014.

claim: In pyrimidine biosynthesis, the rate-limiting step is catalysed by carbamoyl aspartate dehydratase (CAD).
source: In pyrimidine biosynthesis, the rate-limiting step is catalysed by carbamoyl aspartate dehydratase (CAD) (Evans and Guy, 2004), which is also regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of EGFR/RAS/MAP kinase (Makinoshima et al., 2014), Hif 1/2 α (Gordan et al., 2007), or estrogen receptor/Sp1 (Khan et al., 2003) pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Evans and Guy, 2004.

claim: CAD is regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of EGFR/RAS/MAP kinase pathways.
source: In pyrimidine biosynthesis, the rate-limiting step is catalysed by carbamoyl aspartate dehydratase (CAD) (Evans and Guy, 2004), which is also regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of EGFR/RAS/MAP kinase (Makinoshima et al., 2014), Hif 1/2 α (Gordan et al., 2007), or estrogen receptor/Sp1 (Khan et al., 2003) pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Makinoshima et al., 2014.

claim: CAD is regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of Hif 1/2 α pathways.
source: In pyrimidine biosynthesis, the rate-limiting step is catalysed by carbamoyl aspartate dehydratase (CAD) (Evans and Guy, 2004), which is also regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of EGFR/RAS/MAP kinase (Makinoshima et al., 2014), Hif 1/2 α (Gordan et al., 2007), or estrogen receptor/Sp1 (Khan et al., 2003) pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gordan et al., 2007.

claim: CAD is regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of estrogen receptor/Sp1 pathways.
source: In pyrimidine biosynthesis, the rate-limiting step is catalysed by carbamoyl aspartate dehydratase (CAD) (Evans and Guy, 2004), which is also regulated by c-Myc as a response to growth stimulatory signals, such as activation of EGFR/RAS/MAP kinase (Makinoshima et al., 2014), Hif 1/2 α (Gordan et al., 2007), or estrogen receptor/Sp1 (Khan et al., 2003) pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Khan et al., 2003.

claim: c-Myc plays a central role in the control of the metabolism in Chlamydia-infected cells.
source: We recently identified a central role of c-Myc in the control of the metabolism in Chlamydia-infected cells (Rajeeve et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rajeeve et al., 2020.

claim: Chlamydia has a reduced genome and only very limited metabolic capacity.
source: Chlamydia has a reduced genome and only very limited metabolic capacity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydia biology.

claim: Chlamydia has a truncated TCA cycle.
source: For example, they have a truncated TCA cycle and lack the ability to synthesize purine and pyrimidine nucleotides de novo but acquire ATP and nucleosides from the host cell (McClarty and Tipples, 1991; Tipples and McClarty, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McClarty and Tipples, 1991 and Tipples and McClarty, 1993.

claim: Chlamydia lacks the ability to synthesize purine and pyrimidine nucleotides de novo but acquires ATP and nucleosides from the host cell.
source: For example, they have a truncated TCA cycle and lack the ability to synthesize purine and pyrimidine nucleotides de novo but acquire ATP and nucleosides from the host cell (McClarty and Tipples, 1991; Tipples and McClarty, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McClarty and Tipples, 1991 and Tipples and McClarty, 1993.

claim: Expression of IDO and depletion of Trp has been previously described as the main reason for interferon-induced persistence in Chlamydia.
source: Expression of IDO and depletion of Trp has been previously described as the main reason for interferon-induced persistence in Chlamydia (Aiyar et al., 2014; Panzetta et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aiyar et al., 2014 and Panzetta et al., 2018.

claim: Silencing of c-Myc expression prevented normal inclusion formation and chlamydial development.
source: In agreement with our previous results (Rajeeve et al., 2020), silencing of c-Myc expression prevented normal inclusion formation and chlamydial development (Figure 1A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B and C.

claim: Removal of AHT efficiently restored inclusion formation after c-Myc suppression.
source: In contrast to the cells with silenced c-Myc, removal of AHT efficiently restored inclusion formation (Figure 1A, B and C), suggesting that suppression of c-Myc induces a persistence state in Chlamydia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B and C.

claim: Suppression of c-Myc induces a persistence state in Chlamydia.
source: In contrast to the cells with silenced c-Myc, removal of AHT efficiently restored inclusion formation (Figure 1A, B and C), suggesting that suppression of c-Myc induces a persistence state in Chlamydia.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reversibility of the growth inhibition upon c-Myc restoration.

claim: The development of EB was severely affected in condition 3 (continuous c-Myc suppression), but not in the conditions 2 and 4.
source: These so-called secondary infections demonstrated that the development of EB was severely affected in condition 3, but not in the conditions 2 and 4 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: AHT alone did not impact inclusion formation in the absence of c-Myc suppression.
source: AHT alone did not impact inclusion formation in the absence of c-Myc suppression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: IFN-γ-treated cells failed to stabilize c-Myc upon Chlamydia infection.
source: Interestingly, IFN-γ-treated cells failed to stabilize c-Myc upon Chlamydia infection (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Induction of persistence by antibiotic treatment did not alter c-Myc levels.
source: In contrast, induction of persistence by antibiotic treatment, which targets the bacterial rather than host cell metabolism, did not alter c-Myc levels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both IFN-γ and antibiotic treatment caused a failure of the bacteria to produce infectious progenies.
source: Nevertheless, both modes of persistence induction caused a failure of the bacteria to produce infectious progenies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Silencing of c-Myc did not cause significant changes in trpB transcription.
source: However, silencing of c-Myc did not cause significant changes in trpB transcription (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L), indicating that c-Myc depletion does not affect endogenous Trp levels in Ctr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L.

claim: c-Myc depletion does not affect endogenous Trp levels in Ctr.
source: However, silencing of c-Myc did not cause significant changes in trpB transcription (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L), indicating that c-Myc depletion does not affect endogenous Trp levels in Ctr.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of trpB induction, which is a marker of Trp starvation.

claim: Serine 62 phosphorylation (pS62) stabilizes c-Myc.
source: c-Myc protein stability is regulated by two phosphorylation sites with opposing functions. Serine 62 phosphorylation (pS62) stabilizes c-Myc whereas threonine 58 phosphorylation (pT58) promotes c-Myc degradation (Vervoorts et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vervoorts et al., 2006.

claim: Threonine 58 phosphorylation (pT58) promotes c-Myc degradation.
source: c-Myc protein stability is regulated by two phosphorylation sites with opposing functions. Serine 62 phosphorylation (pS62) stabilizes c-Myc whereas threonine 58 phosphorylation (pT58) promotes c-Myc degradation (Vervoorts et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vervoorts et al., 2006.

claim: IFN-γ treatment led to decreased phosphorylation of c-Myc at serine 62.
source: IFN-γ treatment led to decreased phosphorylation of c-Myc at serine 62, a modification that prevents the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the protein (Welcker et al., 2004) while phosphorylation at threonine 58 was unchanged (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Phosphorylation of c-Myc at serine 62 prevents the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the protein.
source: IFN-γ treatment led to decreased phosphorylation of c-Myc at serine 62, a modification that prevents the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the protein (Welcker et al., 2004) while phosphorylation at threonine 58 was unchanged (Figure 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Welcker et al., 2004.

claim: Normalization to c-Myc protein levels revealed strongly increased phosphorylation at Thr58 (4- and 7-fold, IFN-γ and IFN-γ/infected, respectively) and a mild increase at Ser62 (1.3- and 2-fold, IFN-γ and IFN-γ/infected, respectively).
source: However, since c-Myc levels varied significantly upon IFN-γ exposure, normalization to c-Myc protein levels revealed strongly increased phosphorylation at Thr58 (4- and 7-fold, IFN- γ and IFN-γ/infected, respectively) and a mild increase at Ser62 (1.3- and 2-fold, IFN-γ and IFN-γ/infected, respectively).
evidence: This is based on quantification of Western blot data from Figure 1E.

claim: These data are consistent with a role for Thr58 phosphorylation in IFN-γ-mediated downregulation of c-Myc.
source: These data are consistent with a role for Thr58 phosphorylation in IFN-γ-mediated downregulation of c-Myc.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phosphorylation data.

claim: c-Myc was depleted upon IFN-γ treatment of primary cells from human fimbriae (Fimb).
source: c-Myc was also depleted upon IFN-γ treatment of primary cells from human fimbriae (Fimb), although the concentration of IFN-γ required to achieve the same effect was five times higher than in HeLa 229 cells (10 ng/mL in HeLa 229 compared to 50 ng/mL in Fimb) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).

claim: The concentration of IFN-γ required to deplete c-Myc was five times higher in human fimbriae cells than in HeLa 229 cells (10 ng/mL in HeLa 229 compared to 50 ng/mL in Fimb).
source: c-Myc was also depleted upon IFN-γ treatment of primary cells from human fimbriae (Fimb), although the concentration of IFN-γ required to achieve the same effect was five times higher than in HeLa 229 cells (10 ng/mL in HeLa 229 compared to 50 ng/mL in Fimb) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Similar results were obtained with a serovar D strain involved in STD.
source: Similar results were obtained with a serovar D strain involved in STD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Treatment with IFN-γ led to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at serine 727 and tyrosine 701.
source: Treatment with IFN-γ led to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at serine 727 and tyrosine 701 (Figure 1H) and prevented the induction of c-Myc protein (Figure 1H) and mRNA expression (Figure 1F) upon Chlamydia infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: IFN-γ prevented the induction of c-Myc protein upon Chlamydia infection.
source: Treatment with IFN-γ led to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at serine 727 and tyrosine 701 (Figure 1H) and prevented the induction of c-Myc protein (Figure 1H) and mRNA expression (Figure 1F) upon Chlamydia infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: IFN-γ prevented the induction of c-Myc mRNA expression upon Chlamydia infection.
source: Treatment with IFN-γ led to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at serine 727 and tyrosine 701 (Figure 1H) and prevented the induction of c-Myc protein (Figure 1H) and mRNA expression (Figure 1F) upon Chlamydia infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: STAT1 depletion rescued c-Myc levels and chlamydial growth in primary infections.
source: STAT1 depletion rescued c-Myc levels and chlamydial growth in primary infections (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: When bacteria from IFN-γ-treated and STAT1-depleted cells were transferred to fresh cells, infectious progeny could be recovered.
source: When bacteria from IFN-γ-treated and STAT1-depleted cells were transferred to fresh cells, infectious progeny could be recovered, indicating that STAT1 downregulates c-Myc and prevents chlamydial development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, J.

claim: STAT1 downregulates c-Myc and prevents chlamydial development.
source: When bacteria from IFN-γ-treated and STAT1-depleted cells were transferred to fresh cells, infectious progeny could be recovered, indicating that STAT1 downregulates c-Myc and prevents chlamydial development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with STAT1 depletion.

claim: Although c-Myc levels and the bacterial load were slightly reduced upon IFN-α treatment, it failed to induce strong c-Myc depletion and chlamydial persistence.
source: Although c-Myc levels and the bacterial load were slightly reduced upon IFN-α treatment, it failed to induce strong c-Myc depletion and chlamydial persistence suggesting that type I and II IFNs have different effects on c-Myc levels and chlamydial replication (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Type I and II IFNs have different effects on c-Myc levels and chlamydial replication.
source: Although c-Myc levels and the bacterial load were slightly reduced upon IFN-α treatment, it failed to induce strong c-Myc depletion and chlamydial persistence suggesting that type I and II IFNs have different effects on c-Myc levels and chlamydial replication (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of IFN-α and IFN-γ on c-Myc and bacterial growth.

claim: The IFN-γ response in humans and mice is entirely different, limiting the use of murine systems as models for human pathogenic Ctr infections.
source: The IFN-γ response in humans and mice is entirely different, limiting the use of murine systems as models for human pathogenic Ctr infections (Nelson et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nelson et al., 2005.

claim: IFN-γ treatment strongly reduced inclusion formation in human fallopian tube organoids.
source: In this human infection model, IFN-γ treatment strongly reduced inclusion formation (primary infection: Figure 2B) and production of infectious progeny (Figure 2C and F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IFN-γ treatment strongly reduced production of infectious progeny in human fallopian tube organoids.
source: In this human infection model, IFN-γ treatment strongly reduced inclusion formation (primary infection: Figure 2B) and production of infectious progeny (Figure 2C and F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The IFN-γ-STAT1 signalling axis was active in human organoids and efficiently prevented the induction of c-Myc upon infection.
source: Moreover, the IFN-γ-STAT1 signalling axis was active in human organoids and efficiently prevented the induction of c-Myc upon infection (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When IFN-γ was removed by replacing the culture medium, a significant rescue of chlamydial inclusion formation was measured in human organoids.
source: When IFN-γ was removed by replacing the culture medium, a significant rescue of chlamydial inclusion formation was measured (Figure 2D), indicating that this system can be used as a model of persistent infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Human fallopian tube organoids can be used as a model of persistent infection.
source: When IFN-γ was removed by replacing the culture medium, a significant rescue of chlamydial inclusion formation was measured (Figure 2D), indicating that this system can be used as a model of persistent infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the reversibility of persistence upon IFN-γ removal.

claim: Ectopic expression of c-Myc suppressed growth inhibition induced by IFN-γ.
source: Interestingly, ectopic expression of c-Myc suppressed growth inhibition induced by IFN-γ (Figure 3A) and supported the development of infectious progeny (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ectopic expression of c-Myc supported the development of infectious progeny in IFN-γ-treated cells.
source: Interestingly, ectopic expression of c-Myc suppressed growth inhibition induced by IFN-γ (Figure 3A) and supported the development of infectious progeny (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Even after extended exposure of infected cells for 24 hr to IFN-γ, expression of c-Myc rescued progeny formation.
source: Even after extended exposure of infected cells for 24 hr to IFN-γ, expression of c-Myc rescued progeny formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IFN-γ-induced c-Myc downregulation varies in different cell lines.
source: IFN-γ-induced c-Myc downregulation varies in different cell lines and in organoids downregulation is only visible in infected organoids due to weak c-Myc expression in uninfected human organoids (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In organoids, c-Myc downregulation is only visible in infected organoids due to weak c-Myc expression in uninfected human organoids.
source: IFN-γ-induced c-Myc downregulation varies in different cell lines and in organoids downregulation is only visible in infected organoids due to weak c-Myc expression in uninfected human organoids (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Induced expression of c-Myc rescued the strong suppression of infectious progeny development by IFN-γ in fallopian tube organoids.
source: These organoids were then infected with Chlamydia and treated with IFN-γ. Induced expression of c-Myc rescued the strong suppression of infectious progeny development by IFN-γ also in fallopian tube organoids (Figure 3D and E), demonstrating that downregulation of c-Myc is essential for IFN-γ-mediated persistence in this human infection model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Downregulation of c-Myc is essential for IFN-γ-mediated persistence in human fallopian tube organoids.
source: These organoids were then infected with Chlamydia and treated with IFN-γ. Induced expression of c-Myc rescued the strong suppression of infectious progeny development by IFN-γ also in fallopian tube organoids (Figure 3D and E), demonstrating that downregulation of c-Myc is essential for IFN-γ-mediated persistence in this human infection model.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with c-Myc overexpression in organoids.

claim: There is no doubt that Trp plays a central role in the control of chlamydial replication induced by IFN-γ.
source: There is no doubt that Trp plays a central role in the control of chlamydial replication induced by IFN-γ (Byrne et al., 1986; Taylor and Feng, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 1986 and Taylor and Feng, 1991.

claim: The presence of a Trp synthase operon in the genital chlamydial isolates supports a central role of Trp in chlamydial persistence.
source: In the human host, depletion of Trp is the major effector mechanism of IFN-γ and the presence of a Trp synthase operon in the genital chlamydial isolates supports a central role of Trp in chlamydial persistence (Fehlner-Gardiner et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fehlner-Gardiner et al., 2002.

claim: Addition of exogenous Trp rescued chlamydial growth after IFN-γ treatment.
source: As expected, addition of Trp rescued chlamydial growth after IFN-γ treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and gave rise to infectious progeny (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of exogenous Trp gave rise to infectious progeny after IFN-γ treatment.
source: As expected, addition of Trp rescued chlamydial growth after IFN-γ treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and gave rise to infectious progeny (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Addition of Trp resulted in the stabilization of c-Myc, even without chlamydial infection.
source: Surprisingly, addition of Trp also resulted in the stabilization of c-Myc, even without chlamydial infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All Ctr strains are Trp auxotroph but the genital strains retain a Trp synthase (trpB), which uses exogenous indole provided by the microflora in the genital tract as a substrate to synthesize Trp.
source: All Ctr strains are Trp auxotroph but the genital strains retain a Trp synthase (trpB), which uses exogenous indole provided by the microflora in the genital tract as a substrate to synthesize Trp (Byrne et al., 1986; Kari et al., 2011; Østergaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 1986; Kari et al., 2011; Østergaard et al., 2016.

claim: Indole addition resulted in suppression of persistence.
source: Intriguingly, indole addition resulted not only in suppression of persistence (Figure 4B) and formation of infectious progeny (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F), but also in the stabilization of c-Myc in both infected and non-infected cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Indole addition resulted in formation of infectious progeny.
source: Intriguingly, indole addition resulted not only in suppression of persistence (Figure 4B) and formation of infectious progeny (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F), but also in the stabilization of c-Myc in both infected and non-infected cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Indole addition resulted in the stabilization of c-Myc in both infected and non-infected cells.
source: Intriguingly, indole addition resulted not only in suppression of persistence (Figure 4B) and formation of infectious progeny (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F), but also in the stabilization of c-Myc in both infected and non-infected cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The pathogen failed to develop in cells with reduced levels of c-Myc even in presence of excessive exogenous Trp.
source: Interestingly, the pathogen failed to develop in cells with reduced levels of c-Myc even in presence of excessive exogenous Trp (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Chlamydia was unable to establish a secondary infection under low c-Myc expression conditions, irrespective of Trp availability.
source: Furthermore, Chlamydia was also unable to establish a secondary infection under low c-Myc expression conditions, irrespective of Trp availability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Neither chlamydial development nor a secondary infection could be observed in Trp-free medium with constant c-Myc expression.
source: Neither chlamydial development nor a secondary infection could be observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: c-Myc was not stabilized upon chlamydial infection in the absence of Trp.
source: In addition, c-Myc was not stabilized upon chlamydial infection in the absence of Trp (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), suggesting that viable bacteria and Trp are required for the stabilization of c-Myc.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Viable bacteria and Trp are required for the stabilization of c-Myc.
source: In addition, c-Myc was not stabilized upon chlamydial infection in the absence of Trp (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), suggesting that viable bacteria and Trp are required for the stabilization of c-Myc.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of c-Myc stabilization in Trp-free conditions.

claim: IFN-γ, upon binding to its receptor, activates phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and serine-threonine protein kinase (AKT) and induces the dephosphorylation and activation of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3β).
source: IFN-γ, upon binding to its receptor, activates phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and serine-threonine protein kinase (AKT) and induces the dephosphorylation and activation of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3β) (Nguyen et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2001.

claim: If c-Myc is stabilized by the phosphorylation at serine 62 by the MAPK pathway, dephosphorylated active GSK3β phosphorylates c-Myc at threonine 58, followed by its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: If c-Myc is stabilized by the phosphorylation at serine 62 by the MAPK pathway, dephosphorylated active GSK3β phosphorylates c-Myc at threonine 58, followed by its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Albert et al., 1994; Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Albert et al., 1994.

claim: Both the MAPK and PI3K pathways activated during infection are critical for chlamydial development.
source: Both the MAPK and PI3K pathways activated during infection are critical for chlamydial development (Capmany et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2014; Siegl et al., 2014; Subbarayal et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Capmany et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2014; Siegl et al., 2014; Subbarayal et al., 2015.

claim: IFN-γ activated the PI3 kinase pathway as evident from the phosphorylation of AKT.
source: IFN-γ activated the PI3 kinase pathway as evident from the phosphorylation of AKT (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Despite the increase in AKT phosphorylation, IFN-γ treatment caused a reduction of GSK3β phosphorylation and c-Myc levels.
source: Despite this increase in AKT phosphorylation, IFN-γ treatment caused a reduction of GSK3β phosphorylation and c-Myc levels (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The addition of Trp to HeLa 229 or human Fimb cells increased phosphorylation of GSK3β, presumably resulting in its inactivation, and the elevation of c-Myc levels.
source: Surprisingly, the addition of Trp to HeLa 229 or human Fimb cells increased phosphorylation of GSK3β, presumably resulting in its inactivation, and the elevation of c-Myc levels (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Trp rescues chlamydial infection via the activation of the pGSK3β/c-Myc axis.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Trp rescues chlamydial infection via the activation of the pGSK3β/c-Myc axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing Trp-induced GSK3β phosphorylation and c-Myc stabilization.

claim: LAT1 is a system L-amino acid transporter with high affinity for branched chain and bulky amino acids, including Trp.
source: LAT1 is a system L-amino acid transporter with high affinity for branched chain and bulky amino acids, including Trp (Bhutia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bhutia et al., 2015.

claim: The LAT1 promoter has a binding site for c-Myc and it has been shown that overexpression of c-Myc leads to an increased expression of LAT1.
source: Furthermore, the LAT1 promoter has a binding site for c-Myc and it has been shown that overexpression of c-Myc leads to an increased expression of LAT1 (Bhutia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bhutia et al., 2015.

claim: Accumulation of LAT1 protein was detected in a time-dependent manner in infected HeLa 229 cells.
source: Accumulation of LAT1 protein was detected in a time-dependent manner in infected HeLa 229 cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LAT1 protein levels were strongly reduced in IFN-γ-treated cells, irrespective of infection.
source: In contrast, LAT1 protein levels were strongly reduced in IFN-γ-treated cells, irrespective of infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Following c-Myc expression, LAT1 levels in infected cells were rescued even in the presence of IFN-γ.
source: Following c-Myc expression, LAT1 levels in infected cells were rescued even in the presence of IFN-γ (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Trp-degrading enzyme IDO was strongly induced by IFN-γ treatment.
source: Interestingly, the Trp-degrading enzyme IDO, which was strongly induced by IFN-γ treatment as expected, was only partially suppressed by c-Myc expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IDO was only partially suppressed by c-Myc expression.
source: Interestingly, the Trp-degrading enzyme IDO, which was strongly induced by IFN-γ treatment as expected, was only partially suppressed by c-Myc expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibiting IDO1 partially rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence.
source: Whereas inhibiting IDO1 partially rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence (Figure 5D, E and F), it had no effect on the levels of c-Myc (Figure 5D), indicating that rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by IDO1 inhibition does not depend on c-Myc levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, E and F.

claim: IDO1 inhibition had no effect on the levels of c-Myc.
source: Whereas inhibiting IDO1 partially rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence (Figure 5D, E and F), it had no effect on the levels of c-Myc (Figure 5D), indicating that rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by IDO1 inhibition does not depend on c-Myc levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by IDO1 inhibition does not depend on c-Myc levels.
source: Whereas inhibiting IDO1 partially rescued Ctr from IFN-γ-induced persistence (Figure 5D, E and F), it had no effect on the levels of c-Myc (Figure 5D), indicating that rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by IDO1 inhibition does not depend on c-Myc levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rescue without c-Myc level changes.

claim: Chlamydia infection increases intracellular levels of Trp.
source: This analysis showed that Chlamydia infection increases intracellular levels of Trp, while addition of IFN-γ results in decreased Trp levels (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Addition of IFN-γ results in decreased intracellular Trp levels.
source: This analysis showed that Chlamydia infection increases intracellular levels of Trp, while addition of IFN-γ results in decreased Trp levels (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: c-Myc expression in non-infected cells increased intracellular Trp to the levels of infected cells.
source: Interestingly, c-Myc expression in non-infected cells increased intracellular Trp to the levels of infected cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In the presence of IFN-γ, expression of c-Myc only induced a small increase in intracellular Trp levels to about the same level observed in uninfected cells.
source: However, in the presence of IFN-γ, expression of c-Myc only induced a small increase in intracellular Trp levels to about the same level observed in uninfected cells (Figure 5G), indicating that c-Myc expression does not prevent the effect of IFN-γ on Trp degradation.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: c-Myc expression does not prevent the effect of IFN-γ on Trp degradation.
source: However, in the presence of IFN-γ, expression of c-Myc only induced a small increase in intracellular Trp levels to about the same level observed in uninfected cells (Figure 5G), indicating that c-Myc expression does not prevent the effect of IFN-γ on Trp degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics data showing limited Trp restoration.

claim: c-Myc expression had no major effect on Trp uptake in untreated and IFN-γ-treated cells.
source: Unexpectedly, c-Myc expression had no major effect on Trp uptake in untreated and IFN-γ-treated cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data of culture medium shown in Figure 5H.

claim: c-Myc expression strongly enhanced the production of kynurenine in all IFN-γ-treated samples.
source: To our surprise, c-Myc expression strongly enhanced the production of kynurenine in all IFN-γ-treated samples whereas infection alone or in cells with constant c-Myc expression had no effect (Figure 5I), suggesting that the relatively low Trp levels in the IFN-γ-treated, c-Myc-expressing cells depend on an increased turn-over.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The relatively low Trp levels in the IFN-γ-treated, c-Myc-expressing cells depend on an increased turn-over.
source: To our surprise, c-Myc expression strongly enhanced the production of kynurenine in all IFN-γ-treated samples whereas infection alone or in cells with constant c-Myc expression had no effect (Figure 5I), suggesting that the relatively low Trp levels in the IFN-γ-treated, c-Myc-expressing cells depend on an increased turn-over.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased kynurenine production despite low Trp levels.

claim: Restoring Trp metabolism is not the main mechanism of the c-Myc-dependent rescue of chlamydial persistence downstream of IFN-γ signalling.
source: In conclusion, restoring Trp metabolism is not the main mechanism of the c-Myc-dependent rescue of chlamydial persistence downstream of IFN-γ signalling.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics data showing that c-Myc rescue occurs despite continued Trp degradation.

claim: Hierarchical clustering analysis revealed the grouping of all conditions permissive for chlamydial development.
source: Interestingly, hierarchical clustering analysis revealed the grouping of all conditions permissive for chlamydial development (Figure 6A), strongly suggesting that these metabolite profiles are indicative of productive chlamydial infection.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: These metabolite profiles are indicative of productive chlamydial infection.
source: Interestingly, hierarchical clustering analysis revealed the grouping of all conditions permissive for chlamydial development (Figure 6A), strongly suggesting that these metabolite profiles are indicative of productive chlamydial infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering analysis.

claim: Chlamydial development is favoured in an environment with high levels of amino acids (tyrosine, histidine, alanine, homoserine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, threonine, asparagine, glutamate) and TCA (citrate, aconitate, malate, α-ketoglutarate) and urea cycle intermediates (ornithine, citrulline).
source: Chlamydial development is favoured in an environment with high levels of amino acids (tyrosine, histidine, alanine, homoserine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, threonine, asparagine, glutamate) and TCA (citrate, aconitate, malate, α-ketoglutarate) and urea cycle intermediates (ornithine, citrulline) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Chlamydia infection resulted in a significant increase in several TCA cycle (related) intermediates, including aconitate, citrate, α-ketoglutarate, and glutamate.
source: Chlamydia infection resulted in a significant increase in several TCA cycle (related) intermediates, including aconitate, citrate, α-ketoglutarate, and glutamate (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The amino acids aspartate, serine, and glycine, which function as important precursors for TCA cycle anaplerosis and nucleotide biosynthesis, were significantly induced by Chlamydia infection.
source: Furthermore, the amino acids aspartate, serine, and glycine, which function as important precursors for TCA cycle anaplerosis and nucleotide biosynthesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), were also significantly induced by Chlamydia infection, while glutamine showed a trend towards induction that failed to reach statistical significance.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Levels of arginine were strongly reduced upon infection.
source: In contrast, levels of arginine were strongly reduced upon infection, while intracellular levels of the urea cycle metabolites ornithine and citrulline were significantly increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Intracellular levels of the urea cycle metabolites ornithine and citrulline were significantly increased upon infection.
source: In contrast, levels of arginine were strongly reduced upon infection, while intracellular levels of the urea cycle metabolites ornithine and citrulline were significantly increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment of infected cells with IFN-γ lowered the induction of glutamate as well as aspartate, serine, and glycine.
source: Remarkably, treatment of infected cells with IFN-γ lowered the induction of glutamate as well as aspartate, serine, and glycine.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Levels of most TCA cycle metabolites, in particular aconitate, citrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate, were reduced upon IFN-γ treatment.
source: Moreover, levels of most TCA cycle metabolites, in particular aconitate, citrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate, were also reduced upon IFN-γ treatment, suggesting that reprogramming of host cell metabolism is a major part of the IFN-γ response (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Reprogramming of host cell metabolism is a major part of the IFN-γ response.
source: Moreover, levels of most TCA cycle metabolites, in particular aconitate, citrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate, were also reduced upon IFN-γ treatment, suggesting that reprogramming of host cell metabolism is a major part of the IFN-γ response (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the broad metabolic changes observed upon IFN-γ treatment.

claim: Re-expression of c-Myc restored levels of the TCA cycle metabolites citrate, aconitate and α-ketoglutarate, as well as the amino acids glutamine, glutamate, and glycine in IFN-γ-treated infected cells.
source: Interestingly, re-expression of c-Myc restored levels of the TCA cycle metabolites citrate, aconitate and α-ketoglutarate, as well as the amino acids glutamine, glutamate, and glycine in IFN-γ-treated infected cells (Figure 6A and B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that these metabolites are required for Chlamydia development.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6A, B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: These metabolites (citrate, aconitate, α-ketoglutarate, glutamine, glutamate, and glycine) are required for Chlamydia development.
source: Interestingly, re-expression of c-Myc restored levels of the TCA cycle metabolites citrate, aconitate and α-ketoglutarate, as well as the amino acids glutamine, glutamate, and glycine in IFN-γ-treated infected cells (Figure 6A and B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that these metabolites are required for Chlamydia development.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between metabolite restoration and rescue of bacterial growth.

claim: IFN-γ treatment significantly lowered the amounts of ATP and CTP as well as AMP, UMP, and cytidine.
source: Interestingly, IFN-γ treatment significantly lowered the amounts of ATP and CTP as well as AMP, UMP, and cytidine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F and Figure 6C.

claim: This reduction in essential precursors for chlamydial DNA replication may explain why Chlamydia enter persistence in the presence of IFN-γ.
source: This reduction in essential precursors for chlamydial DNA replication may explain why Chlamydia enter persistence in the presence of IFN-γ.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the metabolomics data.

claim: Overexpression of c-Myc enhanced levels of nucleoside triphosphates and strongly increased intracellular levels of adenosine, uridine, and cytidine in IFN-γ-treated cells.
source: In addition, overexpression of c-Myc enhanced levels of nucleoside triphosphates and strongly increased intracellular levels of adenosine, uridine, and cytidine in IFN-γ-treated cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and Figure 6C.

claim: The growth of Chlamydia was rescued by the addition of either DMKG or nucleosides in both WII-U2OS and HeLa 229 cell lines.
source: In both cell lines, the growth of Chlamydia was rescued by the addition of either DMKG or nucleosides and both conditions produced infectious progeny (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: Both DMKG and nucleosides produced infectious progeny.
source: In both cell lines, the growth of Chlamydia was rescued by the addition of either DMKG or nucleosides and both conditions produced infectious progeny (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: Restoration of chlamydial development could be achieved by the sole addition of pyrimidine nucleosides (U+C).
source: Moreover, restoration of chlamydial development could also be achieved by the sole addition of pyrimidine nucleosides (U+C), and to a minor extend also by purine nucleosides (A+G) (Western blot in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Restoration of chlamydial development could be achieved to a minor extent by purine nucleosides (A+G).
source: Moreover, restoration of chlamydial development could also be achieved by the sole addition of pyrimidine nucleosides (U+C), and to a minor extend also by purine nucleosides (A+G) (Western blot in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Purines seem to restore inclusion formation more efficiently than pyrimidines.
source: In contrast, purines seem to restore inclusion formation more efficiently than pyrimidines (bar diagram in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Addition of citrate showed the tendency to rescue chlamydial growth.
source: Furthermore, addition of citrate also showed the tendency to rescue chlamydial growth (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In primary human Fimb cells, the addition of DMKG restored the development of Chlamydia.
source: Even in primary human Fimb cells could the addition of DMKG restore the development of Chlamydia (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: IFN-γ broadly alters the metabolism of host cells to limit the availability of metabolic precursors for pyrimidine and purine biosynthesis to promote chlamydial persistence.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that IFN-γ broadly alters the metabolism of host cells to limit the availability of metabolic precursors for pyrimidine and purine biosynthesis to promote chlamydial persistence.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics data and rescue experiments.

claim: The trpBA mutant lacked expression of TrpA or TrpB.
source: This mutant lacked expression of TrpA or TrpB (Figure 7A) and was resistant to rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by generating Trp from indole (Figure 7B), in line with the phenotype of Trp synthase negative Ctr (Caldwell et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The trpBA mutant was resistant to rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by generating Trp from indole.
source: This mutant lacked expression of TrpA or TrpB (Figure 7A) and was resistant to rescue from IFN-γ-induced persistence by generating Trp from indole (Figure 7B), in line with the phenotype of Trp synthase negative Ctr (Caldwell et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of c-Myc restored growth of the trpBA mutant in the presence of IFN-γ.
source: However, expression of c-Myc restored growth of the trpBA mutant in the presence of IFN-γ (Figure 7C).
